newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HINGIS SHOULDERS FAME LIKE A CHAMPION.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS SHOULDERS FAME LIKE A CHAMPION.

text.p: Fame rests easily on the tiny shoulders of 16-year-old Martina Hingis.

The Swiss prodigy moved a step closer on Thursday to becoming the youngest grand slam champion in the Open era, brushing aside American Mary Joe Fernandez in a little over an hour in the semifinals of the Australian Open.
Hingis's meteoric rise to stardom has sponsors scrambling for their cheque books and her rivals squirming.
But where others have folded after similarly heady starts to their careers, Hingis has reacted with the maturity of the woman she was named after - 18 times grand slam champion Martina Navratilova.
"It's just, it's normal," said Hingis, when asked how she felt about reaching her first grand slam final following her 6-1 6-3 victory over Fernandez.
If she wins on Saturday, Hingis will enter the record books as the youngest champion to lift a grand slam title since amateur Lottie Dod won Wimbledon 110 years ago aged 15 years and 10 months.
The Czechoslovak-born Hingis has not dropped a set in six matches at Melbourne Park, displaying all the skills of a natural winner. Her easy confidence sometimes seems to border on arrogance.
"Somehow it was such an easy match, I played almost perfect," said Hingis.
"I think it was too fast for her and I just played everything back and I was being very aggressive...so somehow it was easy."

Despite standing only 1.67 metres and weighing 53 kg, Hingis strikes the ball with intimidating power and accuracy, and she has the ability to take the ball on the rise which widens the angles of her shots.
"I think she makes you go for more than you have to because she's so quick," said Fernandez, the 14th seed.
On Thursday, Hingis showed no signs of the nerves which caused her to stumble against Romania's Ruxandra Dragomir in the quarter-finals.
In her closest match of the tournament, she was taken to a tie-breaker in the first set before regaining her composure to run away with the match in the second.
It took a brush with danger to shake off the jitters.
On the eve of her quarter-final with Romania's Irina Spirlea, Hingis fell from a horse, Magic Girl, but escaped injury after landing on soft grass.
"It was magic for me," said Hingis, who rates riding the horse as one of her most memorable experiences. "If I'm going to win this tournament, I'm going to buy that horse.
"She just helped me a lot, made the light go on after that fall. Since then I changed completely.
"I haven't made one mistake after that...so I think it's not too bad that I fell from the horse."
Hingis's opponent in the final will be France's Mary Pierce, the 1995 champion who is blazing a comeback trail.
The records show Hingis has not taken a set off Pierce in their only three meetings, the last time on clay in Hamburg last April.

Nine months ago, Hingis was still just another player with title-winning potential, ranked 16 in the world. Tour officials said on Thursday that she would end the week as world number two, regardless of the outcome of Saturday's showdown.
